titre: Dutch Disease: How a Gas Discovery Weakened an Economy
accroche: In 1959, a Dutch farmer stumbles on one of the world's largest gas fields, and his country pays for it in industrial decline.
contenu_vulgarise:
On July 22, 1959, a well begun two months earlier on the land of the farmer Kees Boon, near Slochteren, reveals one of the largest natural gas fields ever discovered in Europe: about 2,740 billion cubic meters of recoverable methane, developed by the Nederlandse Aardolie Maatschappij (NAM), a joint venture between Shell and Esso. The Dutch state, a 40% shareholder in the field against 60% for NAM, finds itself at the head of a windfall that nothing in the country's economy had prepared it to receive.

## The Mechanism: A Currency Too Strong for Industry

Gas exports bring in foreign currency in large quantities, which strengthens the Dutch guilder on the foreign exchange markets. A pricier guilder makes goods manufactured in the Netherlands more expensive to export, and imports cheaper on the domestic market: a double effect that penalizes manufacturing, unable to compete at the same exchange rate as the booming gas sector. Finance Minister Jelle Zijlstra chooses to fold this revenue into the current budget rather than create a separate fund that would have insulated it from the domestic economy: a decision to which part of the Dutch deindustrialization of the 1960s and 1970s is attributed. In 1977, the British weekly The Economist labels the phenomenon “Dutch disease,” and gives it its name for good.

## A Mechanism, Not a Gas Curse

Dutch disease is not specifically Dutch or specifically about gas: the economists W. Max Corden and J. Peter Neary formalized its general mechanism in 1982, under the name of deindustrialization by a booming sector, applicable to any economy that suddenly discovers an abundant resource: oil, ore, or even massive financial aid. The shift lies in what the discovery reveals: a windfall is an economic problem only through the channel by which it spreads, the currency. This is the reasoning Norway applies after its own North Sea oil discoveries: rather than injecting the revenue into the current budget, in 1990 it creates a sovereign wealth fund, today one of the largest in the world, which places most of the oil rent outside the national economy instead of letting it weigh on the exchange rate.

repere.texte: The Groningen field holds about 2,740 billion cubic meters of recoverable gas: one of the largest methane fields ever discovered in Europe.

carte.punch: On a Dutch farmer's land, a well uncovers one of Europe's largest gas fields.
carte.idee: On July 22, 1959, the discovery of the Groningen field enriches the Netherlands in foreign currency and strengthens the guilder: which makes manufactured exports more expensive and weakens the country's industry. In 1977, The Economist dubs this mechanism “Dutch disease.”

quiz.question: Why did the discovery of an immense gas field weaken Dutch manufacturing?
choix: Because gas replaced coal in the country's factories
Because gas revenue strengthened the guilder, making manufactured exports more expensive
Because NAM bought up all the Dutch textile factories
Because the state banned exports of manufactured goods to favor gas
quiz.explication: The influx of foreign currency from gas exports pushes up the guilder's exchange rate; goods made in the Netherlands then become more expensive to export, with no factory buyouts or bans involved.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which budgetary choice by Jelle Zijlstra is associated with Dutch deindustrialization in the 1960s and 1970s?
choix: The ban on exporting gas to neighboring countries
Folding gas revenue into the current budget rather than into a separate fund
The creation of a special tax on manufactured imports
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The article attributes part of the deindustrialization to this budgetary choice by Zijlstra, rather than a separate fund, with no connection to an export ban or a nationalization.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Norway do differently from the Netherlands after its own oil discoveries, according to the article?
choix: It creates a sovereign wealth fund in 1990 that places the oil rent outside the national economy
It bans all oil exports before 2000
It pegs its exchange rate to the Dutch guilder
It too folds the revenue into the current budget, like the Netherlands
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The article contrasts the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund created in 1990, which insulates the oil rent from the exchange rate, with the Dutch choice of folding gas revenue into the current budget.
